candidates.label: Sharon Plain
candidates.support: Pleiades' point for the Sharon Plain is corroborated by Wikidata's independently recorded point for the same feature, and matches the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's description of a coastal strip running between the mountains and the Mediterranean, from south of Jaffa north to Mount Carmel.

summary.text: The Sharon is the coastal plain of central Israel, running between the central hill country and the Mediterranean Sea from near Jaffa in the south to Mount Carmel in the north. Acts describes "all who lived at Lydda and in Sharon" turning to the Lord after the apostle Peter healed a paralyzed man there.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the plain's deep, rich soil, its perennial streams, and a once-extensive oak forest in its northern part, and records that the Old Testament pictures Sharon as excellent pasture land, where King David kept royal herds.

scripture.textWEB: All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

otConnections.note: Shitrai the Sharonite is named as the official over King David's herds that fed in Sharon.
Isaiah names "the excellency of Carmel and Sharon" among signs of future restoration and glory.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
